items.excerpt: 08 November 2026• Update: 08 November 2026 Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start Sunday, including Poland's interior minister's claim that far-right ideologies may have influenced a Krakow attacker; Israeli President Isaac Herzog's appointment of Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government; and the US army's announcement of a new task force to disrupt Iran's supply routes. Initial indications suggest that the suspect who opened fire in central Krakow, Poland's second-largest city, was influenced by far-right ideologies, according to Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski. Kierwinski told a news conference that police opened fire on the suspect three minutes after receiving the first report of the attack. He confirmed that six people were killed, including one foreign national, while 16 were injured, including five foreign nationals, two police officers and the suspect. - Israel’s President Herzog says he will task Eisenkot with forming next government Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced that he will task Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming the next government, Israeli news site Ynet reported. Eisenkot has been invited to receive the mandate at a ceremony at the President’s Residence on Sunday at 5 pm local time (1500GMT), according to the report. Once he receives the mandate, Eisenkot will have 28 days to form a government. Herzog can grant an extension of up to 14 days under Israel’s Basic Law. - US army announces new task force to disrupt Iran’s supply routes The US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) announced the establishment of a new task force aimed at disrupting Iran’s use of land routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials, expanding Washington’s pressure on Tehran. In a statement on US social media platform X, CENTCOM said Adm. Brad Cooper, the command’s chief, directed the formation of Task Force Iron Gate on Nov. 7. The unit, comprising approximately 20 civilian and military personnel, will be based in Tampa, Florida. The task force will work with other US government agencies to monitor and prevent the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and what Washington describes as illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.

items.excerpt: Israel’s president taps opposition candidate Eisenkot to form a government, in setback for Netanyahu JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli President Isaac Herzog said Saturday night that he was giving opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form a governing coalition following elections on Oct. 27. He has up to six weeks to form a coalition, a challenging task in a deeply divided country reeling from the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks and the three years of wars that have followed in Gaza and beyond. In discussions with the president this week, representatives from most of Israel’s main parties recommended Eisenkot be tasked with assembling a new government. But putting together the parliamentary majority needed remains fraught and any possible coalition would require candidates to make tough compromises that could outrage their own voters. WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White, an announcement unconventional even for the norm-busting president. White said Saturday that he plans to meet with Trump on Monday at the White House. Trump, while he was at his golf club in Florida, posted on social media that he made the offer to “the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior” to become the Republican president's chief spokesperson. White, who was in London on Saturday for a boxing event, was asked at a news conference about Trump's post and responded by saying that he planned to fly to Washington right after and meet with Trump on Monday. KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — A Polish man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow on Saturday and opened fire, killing six people and injuring 15 others before police shot and wounded him, authorities said. The attack, which Poland’s defense minister described as an “act of terror,” happened in Main Square, which is in the heart of Krakow’s Old Town and is a major tourist hub in the country’s second-largest city. The 25-year-old attacker drove to multiple spots in the square and opened fire at each stop with an automatic weapon, authorities said. Although they didn’t release his name, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the man holds “very radical” and “ultranationalistic” views. Hours after the attack, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities found the bodies of three of the suspect's close family members — two women and a man — inside of his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow.

items.title: Fed policymakers consider rate hike after strong jobs report - The Korea Herald
items.excerpt: # Fed policymakers consider rate hike after strong jobs report Published : Nov. 8, 2026 - 10:24:06 Hiring signs are displayed in Wheeling, Illinois, Oct. 14. AP-Yonhap A stronger-than-expected US jobs report bolstered the case for further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, which had lost some momentum ‌amid a post-election stock market selloff and growing fears that weaker AI-driven demand could undercut the economy. Employers added 165,000 jobs last month, more than twice what economists had expected, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said Friday, and the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent. Average hourly wages gained 3.1 percent from a year earlier, not enough to keep up with a 3.7 percent rise in consumer prices that is ‌taking a bigger chunk of the typical paycheck's purchasing power. After the US central bank left its policy rate on hold last month, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said policymakers would be watching for "the accumulation of data" to help decide whether more monetary policy tightening would be needed. For San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly, the latest monthly jobs report appeared to put a definitive tick in the "yes" column. "People are just at the point where they're — they say 'Inflation — I'm doing well ⁠in everything, except I can't keep up with inflation,' so that has to be our number one priority, and the fact that we have a solid labor market gives us the latitude, really, to just get that job done," Daly said in an interview on CNBC. "My expectation is, we're going to have to tighten policy further," said Daly, who is not a voting member of the Fed's policy committee this ⁠year but typically voices views similar to the majority view. Noting "how volatile the world seems to be in many ways," she added, "those volatilities are something that you have to take into account, collect more information, and be deliberate but more gradual in how you get there when you don't know exactly where you're going to need to head. But more is likely to be ​needed and certainly we're prepared — I'm prepared — to do that, if that's what the economy calls for." In comments at a St. Louis civic event Friday, St. ‌Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said inflation remained the top concern in his conversations with businesses in his district. "Inflation is a regressive tax, a distortionary tax," said Musalem, who has advocated for further rate ‌increases. "The best thing we can do for growth ‌and employment is bring inflation back down on a timely basis." He did not address a recent swoon in stock markets driven lower by new doubts about ‌the pace and sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom, but said for now he feels the emerging ​industry is feeding higher inflation through demand for commodities such as copper. Even if that pays off in future profit and productivity, "we need to make monetary policy for the economy of the day, not what it may be ⁠five years from now," Musalem said, and on that basis, for now at least, AI investment "will continue to contribute to inflation." ... The Nasdaq Composite index fell by the most in 19 months on Thursday as the extent of the political shift in the US became apparent ​after Democrats won control of Congress and emerged victorious in a clutch of gubernatorial races in the midterm elections on Tuesday. Several of the victorious Democratic gubernatorial candidates ran on promises to rein in data center construction, and ... The jitters over AI also prompted traders to back away from what had been big bets on a ⁠Fed rate hike next month, figuring that a slowdown in AI-related demand could cool economic growth and ease inflationary pressures, ⁠making further monetary policy tightening a ⁠less urgent matter. The ‌release of the latest employment report, however, put a Fed rate hike back in focus. Markets were pricing about an 80 percent chance of a quarter-percentage-point policy rate increase at the Fed's December 8-9 meeting, up from about 67 percent Thursday. Traders now also see the next and final rate increase coming earlier, in April instead of June, as the central bank battles inflation that has been running above its 2 percent target for more than ​five years. "This is a very strong labor market report on the heels of solid GDP and consumer spending data last week, reinforcing the economy's positive momentum," Olu Sonola, an analyst at Fitch Ratings, wrote after the report. Recent concern over AI poses a risk to that outlook, Sonola said, "but for now the economy remains on firm footing. The labor market's resilience keeps the Fed focused on inflation and pushes the policy debate further toward a December rate hike." (Reuters)

items.title: U.S. Companies' Inflation Concerns Reach Highest Level in Over Two Years | Aju Press
items.excerpt: **by BAE IN SUN** *Posted : November 8, 2026, 15:04**Updated : November 8, 2026, 15:04* U.S. companies' concerns about inflation have surged to their highest level in over two years. Rising oil prices, increased raw material costs, and logistics expenses are intensifying cost pressures on businesses, drawing attention to key U.S. inflation indicators set to be released this week. In last month's series of third-quarter earnings reports, inflation was a central topic. According to Bloomberg, companies in the S&P 500 mentioned the term 'inflation' 820 times during their October earnings calls, marking the highest monthly count since February 2024. In the first week of November, mentions of inflation by companies have already surpassed the total for November of last year, Bloomberg reported. By sector, industrial companies, which include machinery, equipment, construction, and transportation, had the highest number of inflation mentions at 213. Basic materials companies, including steel, chemicals, and metals, followed with 135 mentions. This reflects companies' concerns about rising production and operational costs due to raw material and energy prices, as well as logistics expenses. The impact of inflation is also spreading to consumer goods companies. U.S. automaker General Motors (GM) projected that rising raw material, logistics, and memory semiconductor prices will lead to approximately $2 billion in additional costs this year. Of this, about $400 million is attributed to inflation, with most of the impact expected to occur in the fourth quarter. As companies face increasing cost burdens, there are concerns that inflationary pressures at the production level will translate into consumer prices. If inflation rises again, it could influence the Federal Reserve's monetary policy. According to the CME FedWatch on November 6, the futures market reflects a 76.33% probability that the Fed will raise interest rates by 0.25 percentage points at its December Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, up from 66.9% the previous day. Inflation pressures are expected to be confirmed in the key U.S. inflation indicators set to be released this week. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) for October will be published on November 10, with the market anticipating a 0.3% increase from the previous month, a slowdown from September's 0.6% rise. However, due to a government shutdown in October 2025, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) was unable to collect price survey data, meaning there will be no year-over-year increase reported this time. Following that, the Producer Price Index (PPI) for October will be released on November 13. Bloomberg forecasts that the October PPI will rise by 6.6% compared to the same month last year, exceeding the previous month's increase of 6.3%. If market expectations hold, this would represent the highest level in nearly four years. The PPI, also known as wholesale prices, reflects changes in the prices businesses receive for producing and selling goods and services. Increases in production-level prices can affect companies' costs and selling prices, ultimately impacting consumer prices, making it a key indicator for gauging inflation trends.

items.title: US Inflation Is Climbing Again — Tuesday's Report Shows How Far It Spreads | AInvest
items.excerpt: Generated by Charles Hayes Reviewed by The Newsroom Sat, Nov 7, 2026, 23:57:49 ET 3min read ... The last inflation report before the Fed's year-end decision lands Tuesday at 8:30 a.m. ET, and it walks into a debate that barely existed two months ago. The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the October Consumer Price Index, the annual, year-over-year number that most people simply call "inflation." The setup matters far more than the usual monthly routine: after a long drift back down, the annual rate has turned up again, and markets have swung from treating the inflation fight as largely won to pricing a rate hike. Here is the re-acceleration in two numbers. The Bureau of Labor Statistics put September's annual CPI at 3.7%, up from 3.4% in August and a tick above expectations; it was 3.0% a year earlier. And the Fed's preferred gauge, the PCE price index, ran at 3.6% in September in Commerce Department data, with the core reading that strips out food and energy at 3.1%. The consequential part is not the fraction of a point — it is the duration underneath. September marked the 68th straight month that PCE inflation has sat above the Fed's 2% target, a streak that had no precedent in the modern inflation-targeting era that began in 2012. ... Oil has fallen almost 20% in a week to below $100 a barrel on hopes the Iran war is de-escalating, even as it stays up almost 60% for the year. ... Headline inflation is noisy precisely because energy shoves it around; the Fed's map for the durable trend is core, which removes food and energy. September's core PCE was 3.1% against a 3.6% headline.

items.title: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
items.excerpt: Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms. The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump. But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office. The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans". Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy. "There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said. The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away. It's too early to tell which faction will win out. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.

items.title: Adam Driver wont return for Girls reboot | Mint
items.excerpt: PTI Published 8 Nov 2026, 09:48 AM IST Adam Driver wont return for Girls reboot Los Angeles, Nov 8 (PTI) Actor Adam Driver won't return to reprise his role in the reboot of the 2012 series "Girls", which served as a breakthrough for him. The actor starred as Adam Sackler in the original series, which concluded in 2017 after nine seasons. The announcement of the reboot had fans thinking if the actor will step into Sackler's shoes again. When asked about the return to the series, Driver confirmed he isn't in the project. "No, but I wish them the best of luck," he told Cinema Blend in an interview. The series revolved around four twenty-something women navigating the messy, awkward, and often humiliating realities of post-collegiate life in New York City. It featured Lena Dunham as Hannah Horvat, Lena Allison Williams as Michael , Jemima Kirke as Jessa Johansson and Zosia Mamet in the role of Shoshanna Shapiro, among others. "Girls" was created by Lena Dunham, who is returning for the reboot series, which will comprise five episodes. Williams, Kirke, Mamet (Shoshanna), and Andrew Rannells are also set to return for the series.

items.title: Emma Stone Joins 'The Catch' Co-Star Druski During His 'Saturday Night Live' Opening Monologue, Jokes He Misread Scenes In Their Movie - Watch Now! | Just Jared - Celebrity News, Entertainment News & Photos
items.excerpt: AJ Pitts Nov 8, 2026 · 2 min read Credit: Saturday Night Live/NBC **Emma Stone** returned to the ***Saturday Night Live*** stage this weekend! The 38-year-old actress, who hosted the show five times, joined this week’s host **Druski** during his opening monologue on Saturday night (November 7). If you didn’t know, they are set to co-star in the upcoming movie, *The Catch*. “I am living proof you can bet on yourself and make your dreams come true,” **Druski** said in his monologue. “I just finished filming my first-ever movie with **Emma Stone** and she is right now.” > Druski’s monologue! https://t.co/RnaI5AkQpb > — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) November 8, 2026 After she walked on stage, **Druski** said, “I’m actually playing her love interest in the new movie that we just did.” “I think you might have misread that in those scenes, because we weren’t love interests in the film,” **Emma **replied. “But now it is starting to make more sense why you kept looking at me like that for all those scenes.” “That’s probably why we ain’t kiss either,” he said, to which she said, “Yeah.” “If there’s a part two, we’ll get it done,” **Druski** added. ... ### What is *The Catch* about? **Emma** and **Druski**‘s upcoming movie is actually being directed by her husband, **Dave McCary**. Plot details are currently being kept under wraps, but it is said to be a baseball rom-com in the vein of *Bull Durham* and *Notting Hill*, according to *Deadline*, and **Emma** plays “the most hated woman in baseball.” They also say **Druski** will play ** Emma**‘s security guard in the film. **Chris Pine** also stars, along with *Saturday Night Live*‘s **Ashley Padilla** as **Emma**‘s sister.
